newsitem.title: UK: Playboy businessman Hanson keeps top job in family.
newsitem.headline: Playboy businessman Hanson keeps top job in family.

text.p: A one-time playboy who escorted film stars around 1950s London and became one of Britain's top industrialists, 74-year-old Lord Hanson capped his career in 1997 by completing plans to split up the company he co-founded 46 years earlier.

With the demerger process finalised in February, Lord Hanson announced on Thursday he planned to step down as chairman of "new Hanson" at the close of 1997 and appointed as his successor Chris Collins -- currently deputy chairman and married to the chief's niece.
The anointed successor of the FTSE 100 building group which inherited the Hanson name as part of the conglomerate carve-up, pledges to remain true to the current strategy and spirit of management.
But Collins' appointment flags the close of the old era.

The demerger plan for Hanson Plc, announced early last year, was the final surprise delivered to shareholders after decades of deal-making that turned the industrial conglomerate that Lord Hanson chaired into one of the largest companies in both Britain and the United States.

By acquiring interests ranging from chemicals and tobacco to energy and building through a series of takeover battles on both sides of the Atlantic, Hanson, along with co-founder the late Lord White, won a reputation as a brilliant businessman.

The 1980s saw the full might of the Hanson takeover machine swing into operation, with the 2.5 billion pound ($3.9 billion) bid for Imperial Tobacco and the $930 million purchase of the SCM Chemicals group, both in 1986.
That was followed a year later by the $1.6 billion purchase of the Kidde fire equipment business and in 1989 by the 3.3 billion pound purchase of Consolidated Goldfields.

The pace hardly let up in the 1990s, with the $2.3 billion acquisition of U.S. group Quantum Chemical in 1993 and last year's controversial purchase of Britain's largest electricity distributor, Eastern Group, for 2.5 billion pounds.

It was all a far cry from the playboy whose picture regularly adorned the gossip columns of the 1950s. Hanson was then best known for his highly-publicised liaisons with actresses Jean Simmons and Joan Collins and he was engaged to Audrey Hepburn for almost a year.

Hanson's introduction to this glamorous set came from a family love of horses. His father's patronage of young showjumpers gave the family an entree to the equine world and the social world beyond it, a friend later recalled.

But in the background Hanson was busy using the transport company he inherited from his father, a wealthy northern entrepreneur, as the base for what was to emerge as a conglomerate worth close to 11 billion pounds ($16.5 billion).

His growth philosophy was remarkably simple. He aimed to buy undervalued, unglamorous companies, steering clear of competitive high-technology fields, and then improved performance by ejecting managers and cutting costs.

Gordon White, who died last year, meanwhile set up the U.S. arm, Hanson Industries, and expanded it into an operation making up a sizeable part of group sales and profits, which came to 286 million pounds at the operating level last year.

Hanson played a key role in the 1986 struggle over the future of Britain's ailing Westland Helicopter company, which led to the resignation of two ministers and embarrassed the government of Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.

At a critical moment in the battle, Hanson suddenly acquired a 15 per cent stake in the company and committed his votes to a U.S.-led rescue package, tipping the balance against a rival West European consortium.

But Hanson's style has also attracted critics. During Imperial's struggle against his unwanted takeover bid, a spokesman for Imperial said: "Lord Hanson buys companies well and sells companies well, but he manages them very badly. He buys, squeezes and goes on to the next one."

From the end of the 1980s Hanson concentrated on selling parts of recent acquisitions -- a move that in retrospect foreshadowed the final demerger. He pared down Imperial Group by disposing of its leisure and food operations, including major brewer Courage, so that virtually only its core tobacco business remained in Hanson control.

In the United States, Hanson disposed of parts of Kaiser cement, which it bought in March 1987, and fire extinguishers to aircraft parts manufacturer Kidde Inc, acquired in August the same year. And last year it said it was selling its Cavenham Forest Industries and Suburban Propane businesses for a total $1.5 billion.
The demerger was a bid to bring out further value from the shares by allowing the diverse collection of interests built up over the years to grow within four more tightly-focused businesses.
But in the run-up to demerger, shares in the group had languished, triggering the break-up.
Born on January 20, 1922, James Edward Hanson is an outspoken rightwinger and a major contributor to Conservative Party funds.
One of Britain's most highly-paid executives, he was created a peer by Margaret Thatcher in 1983 in recognition of his services to industry.
